transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: A new study published in the journal *Pediatrics* has found that children who spend more time outdoors have significantly better eyesight and lower rates of nearsightedness compared to children who stay indoors most of the time. The research, which followed over 2,000 primary school children for three years, found that those who spent at least two hours outside every day were 30 percent less likely to develop myopia, or nearsightedness, than children who spent less than one hour outdoors daily. Researchers believe that natural daylight and looking at objects in the distance help the eye develop properly in childhood. The study also found that it didn't matter what children were doing outside—playing sports, walking, or just sitting in the sun all had the same protective effect. Eye doctors are now recommending that parents make sure their children get regular outdoor time to protect their vision, especially as more and more children spend time looking at screens and doing close-up work like reading and homework.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: The city of Edinburgh in Scotland has become the first in the United Kingdom to introduce a "tourist tax" on visitors staying in hotels and other accommodation. The new charge, which began this month, adds two pounds per person per night to the cost of hotel rooms, hostels, and even Airbnb rentals. The city council says the tax will raise approximately 15 million pounds per year, which will be used to fund public services, maintain tourist attractions, and keep the city clean and welcoming for visitors. The tax has been controversial—hotel owners argue it will make Edinburgh more expensive and drive tourists away to other cities, while supporters say that visitors should contribute to the cost of running the city they enjoy. Similar tourist taxes already exist in many European cities including Paris, Rome, and Barcelona, and other UK cities including London and Manchester are considering introducing their own versions. Early data from the first month shows that hotel bookings have not decreased significantly, suggesting the tax has not deterred visitors.
Questions 3 to 5 are based on the news report you have just heard.
3. What new policy has Edinburgh introduced?
4. How will the money from the tax be used?
5. What concern do hotel owners have about the tax?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: Scientists at the University of California have developed a new type of solar panel that can generate electricity from rain as well as sunlight, making it possible to produce clean energy even on cloudy or rainy days. The panels work by using a special coating that generates a small electric charge when raindrops hit and roll down the surface, taking advantage of the kinetic energy of falling rain. While the amount of electricity produced from rain is much less than from sunlight—only about 10 percent of what a traditional solar panel produces on a sunny day—it means the panels can still generate some power during bad weather and at night when it rains. Researchers say the technology could be especially useful in places with high rainfall and limited sunshine, such as parts of northern Europe and Southeast Asia. The panels are still in the experimental stage, but the team hopes to have a commercial product available within five years. They are also working on improving the efficiency of the rain energy generation to make the panels even more useful.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Mia): Hey Jake, I need your advice. I'm thinking about getting a pet, but I can't decide what kind of animal to get. What do you think—cat or dog?

Man (Jake): That's a big decision, Mia. Both are great, but they're very different. First, how much time do you have every day to spend with a pet? Dogs need a lot of attention—you have to walk them at least twice a day, play with them, and they get lonely if you're gone all day. Cats are much more independent.
Woman: That's a good point. I work full-time, so I'm out of the house from about 9 AM to 6 PM every weekday. I don't want to get a pet that would be miserable being alone all day.

Man: Then a cat might be a better fit for you. They're perfectly happy to sleep and look out the window while you're at work, and they'll be excited to see you when you get home. But you still have to play with them and give them attention every evening. What about your apartment—does your landlord allow pets?

Woman: Yeah, I checked, and pets are allowed as long as they're not too big. I live in a one-bedroom apartment, so space is kind of limited. That's another reason I was thinking a cat might be better—they don't need as much room as a big dog.

Man: Definitely. A small dog could work too, like a Chihuahua or a French Bulldog, but even small dogs need walks and training. Cats are easier in that way—you just need a litter box, food, water, and some toys.
Woman: What about the cost? I've heard pets can be really expensive, especially with vet bills.

Man: That's true for both, but dogs are usually more expensive overall. They need more food, you might have to pay for dog walkers or daycare, and vet bills can be higher. Cats are generally cheaper to take care of, but you still need to budget for regular checkups, vaccinations, and unexpected medical costs.
Woman: Hmm, okay. I think I'm leaning toward a cat then. Should I get a kitten or an adult cat from a shelter?

Man: Oh, you should definitely adopt from a shelter! There are so many cats that need homes. Kittens are cute, but they're a lot of work—they have tons of energy, they scratch things, and they need more supervision. Adult cats are often calmer, already litter-trained, and their personalities are more developed so you know what you're getting.
Woman: That makes sense. I think I'll go to the animal shelter this weekend and see if there's a cat that connects with me. Thanks for your advice, Jake!
Man: No problem! Let me know when you get one—I'd love to come meet your new cat.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The history of the bicycle spans over two hundred years, and this simple invention has had an enormous impact on transportation, society, and even women's rights. The earliest version of the bicycle, called the "draisine," was invented in Germany in 1817 by Baron Karl von Drais. It had two wheels and a frame, but no pedals—riders pushed themselves along with their feet, like a modern balance bike.

Pedal-powered bicycles didn't appear until the 1860s, when French inventors added pedals to the front wheel. These early bicycles, nicknamed "boneshakers" because of their rough ride on cobblestone streets, had wheels of equal size and were made entirely of wood and iron. They were followed in the 1870s by the high-wheel bicycle, also known as the "penny-farthing," which had a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel. These were fast but dangerous—riders sat high above the front wheel and could be thrown forward over the handlebars if they hit a bump.

The modern bicycle as we know it today appeared in the 1880s with the "safety bicycle," which had two equal-sized wheels, a chain drive to the rear wheel, and pneumatic rubber tires. This design was much safer, more comfortable, and easier to ride, and it led to a huge bicycle boom in the 1890s. Suddenly, millions of people could travel quickly and cheaply without relying on horses or trains.

For women in particular, the bicycle was revolutionary. It gave them unprecedented freedom of movement, allowing them to travel independently without chaperones. It also led to changes in women's clothing—long, heavy dresses and corsets were impractical for cycling, so women began wearing more comfortable, practical clothing, which was controversial at the time. Many historians consider the bicycle an important factor in the women's liberation movement of the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

Today, bicycles remain one of the most efficient and environmentally friendly forms of transportation ever invented, used by billions of people around the world for commuting, exercise, and recreation.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Many people think that the ability to speak and understand language is something unique to humans, but research over the past few decades has shown that many animals have surprisingly complex communication systems. While they may not have grammar or syntax the way human languages do, animals use a variety of sounds, gestures, and signals to convey detailed information to each other.

One of the most well-studied examples is the honeybee. When a forager bee finds a good source of nectar, it returns to the hive and performs a special "waggle dance" that tells other bees exactly where the food is. The direction of the dance indicates the direction relative to the sun, and the length of the dance tells the distance—each second of waggling represents about one kilometer of distance. The bee can even communicate information about the quality of the food source by how enthusiastically it dances.

Prairie dogs, small rodents that live in underground colonies in North America, have an even more sophisticated alarm call system. Researchers have found that prairie dogs have different warning calls for different types of predators—hawks, coyotes, snakes, and humans all get distinct calls. Even more remarkably, their calls can include details about size, color, and speed—they can communicate not just "there's a human coming," but "there's a tall human wearing a blue shirt walking slowly." This level of detail in animal communication was previously thought to be impossible.

Dolphins also have complex communication, including signature whistles that function like names—each dolphin has a unique whistle that it uses to identify itself, and dolphins will respond when they hear their own signature whistle played back. They also appear to use body language, touch, and a variety of other sounds to communicate.

While scientists agree that these communication systems are not the same as human language, studying them helps us understand how language evolved and what aspects of language are truly unique to humans. It also shows that intelligence and communication come in many different forms across the animal kingdom.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: Sleep is something we spend about a third of our lives doing, yet most people don't fully understand why we need it or how important it is for our physical and mental health. While we sleep, our bodies are far from inactive—they're busy performing essential maintenance and repair functions that keep us healthy.

Physically, sleep is when our bodies repair damaged cells, build muscle and bone, and strengthen the immune system. Growth hormone, which is essential for growth in children and for tissue repair in adults, is released primarily during deep sleep. Sleep also helps regulate hormones that control appetite, metabolism, and blood sugar. Studies have shown that people who don't get enough sleep are more likely to gain weight, develop type 2 diabetes, and have weakened immune systems that make them more susceptible to colds and infections.

Mentally, sleep is just as important. During sleep, especially during the REM (rapid eye movement) stage when we dream, our brains process and consolidate memories from the day, transferring information from short-term to long-term memory. This is why getting a good night's sleep before an exam is more effective than pulling an all-nighter cramming—your brain needs sleep to actually store the information you've studied. Sleep also helps with problem-solving and creativity—many people have had the experience of waking up with the solution to a problem they were stuck on the day before.

Unfortunately, sleep deprivation is extremely common in modern society. Many adults regularly get less than the recommended seven to nine hours of sleep per night, and teenagers and college students are even more likely to be sleep-deprived due to busy schedules, screen time, and irregular sleep patterns. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to serious health problems including heart disease, depression, anxiety, and even a shorter lifespan.

The good news is that improving your sleep habits can have dramatic positive effects on your health and well-being. Simple changes like going to bed and waking up at the same time every day, avoiding screens before bed, keeping your bedroom cool and dark, and avoiding caffeine in the afternoon can significantly improve sleep quality. Prioritizing sleep isn't lazy—it's one of the most important things you can do for your health.
